p:cNvPr.descr: A few diagrams showing examples and structures of GFP (green fluorescent protein). (a) A photograph of the bioluminescent jellyfish Aequorea victoria. The jellyfish glows blue on a black background. It has a large, domed clear bell on top, with large glowing curved lines following the shape of the bell. The tentacles are long, wispy, and thin, and glow blue as well. (b) To the right is the protein structure of the GFP and the fluorophore which makes bioluminescence possible. The GFP itself has a right-twisting barrel structure made of beta strands, shown as greenish gray arrows. There are long, thin gray residues coming off the top and bottom of the barrel. In the center of the barrel is the fluorophore (labeled above), which is a lumpy green protein which casts a green glow over the barrel. (c) To the right, the structural rearrangements resulting in the formation of a fluorophore. This is a simplified structure and does not actually indicate the presence of carbon with a C when it is bonded only to other carbons; but carbons will be listed in the description for clarity. Therefore, the connection of two or more bonds, which is not otherwise labeled, contains a carbon (C). The diagram begins with the immature structure. It begins on the left with a benzene ring which bonds down and left to OH. This is labeled Tyr below. The benzene ring bonds right to carbon, which bonds down and right to carbon, which bonds down to NH and up and right to carbon, which double bonds up to O and down and right to N (which has two red dots representing electrons on it), which bonds up and right to Gly. Gly has a long wavy chain coming off to its right. The previously mentioned NH bonds down and right to carbon, which double bonds up and right to O and down to Ser, which has a wavy chain coming down from it. The red-dotted N transfers electrons, shown by a red arrow, down to the double bond of the O, which then results in production of an H+ to the right. Below is a down and right arrow with a divergent arrow to the right, labeled H2O, indicating its removal. The structure below is still the same benzene ring bonded down and left to OH and bonded right to carbon, but now that carbon bonds right to a 5-sided ring. It bonds right to carbon, which bonds down to N, which double bonds right to carbon, which bonds down and right to Ser and up to N. N bonds right to Gly and up and left to carbon, which double bonds up to O. Gly and Ser both have wavy chains coming off their ends. Below there is a down arrow with a down arrow attached to a right-curved down arrow labeled “multiple steps.” Its upper end is labeled, “O2”; its bottom end is labeled “H2O2.” Finally there is the structure of the mature fluorophore. The structure below is still the same benzene ring bonded down and left to OH and bonded right to carbon, but now that carbon double bonds right to a 5-sided ring. It double bonds right to carbon, which bonds down to N, which double bonds right to carbon, which bonds down and right to Ser and up to N. N bonds right to Gly and up and left to carbon, which double bonds up to O. Gly and Ser both have wavy chains coming off their ends. (d) A row of test tubes filled with bioluminescent variants of GFP in multiple colors. They are against a black background to better show their glow. A large spectrum of colors is shown, beginning at the left with a deep blue, then through a lighter blue, then through two shades of green, then to yellow and then to orange, then into salmon pink and deep cerise, then into fuchsia and deep crimson to the right. (e) A microscopic image of the body of a bioluminescent worm. It is clear and against a black background. The worm is curled into a U-shape with the bottom of the U toward the lower right. The head is tapered, on the right side; the tail is also tapered, on the left. Both are labeled. The inside surface of the U is labeled dorsal; the outside of the U is labeled ventral. Just below the head there is a cluster of bright green glowing proteins. Below this and all the way around the loop of the U are tiny, pink, glowing proteins. Toward the tail there is a single green glowing dot. To the right is a photograph of some fluorescent E. coli cells. To the top are single cells, rod-shaped; to the bottom there are two pairs of cells bonded together at the ends. The cells have glowing red cell walls around their edges and glowing green dots inside. Two cells at the bottom left and one cell at the top right each have two glowing green dots inside.
